shorts.title: His Parents Bet $245,000 on Amazon
shorts.description: In 1995, Jeff Bezos told his parents there was a 70% chance they'd lose their money. They invested anyway.
sources: Wikipedia: Jeff Bezos — early Amazon funding
Bezos interviews about the 70% risk warning

scenes.text: In 1995, Jeff Bezos asked his parents for money for a tiny online bookstore.
He warned them: there's about a seventy percent chance you lose all of it.
They invested anyway. Around two hundred and forty five thousand dollars.
That bookstore was Amazon.
That bet turned into billions of dollars for the Bezos family.
Would you have bet on your kid?

shorts.title: He Sold an Internet Radio Site for $5.7 Billion
shorts.description: In 1999, Yahoo bought Mark Cuban's Broadcast.com for $5.7 billion in stock. Then the bubble popped.

scenes.text: Mark Cuban sold a website for five point seven billion dollars. At the perfect moment.
His company, Broadcast.com, streamed radio and sports over the internet. In the nineties, that was magic.
In 1999, at the peak of the dot com craze, Yahoo bought it, paying in stock.
Cuban protected his shares so a crash couldn't wipe him out.
Months later, the bubble burst, and Yahoo eventually shut Broadcast.com down.
Cuban walked away a billionaire. Timing is everything.

shorts.title: From $5,000 to Billionaire: Spanx
shorts.description: Sara Blakely cut the feet off her pantyhose and built a billion-dollar company with her savings.
sources: Forbes, March 2012: youngest self-made female billionaire

scenes.text: She cut the feet off her pantyhose, and became a billionaire.
Sara Blakely was selling fax machines door to door.
She wanted something smooth to wear under white pants, so she grabbed scissors and made it herself.
With five thousand dollars of savings, she started Spanx in 2000.
Factories laughed at her idea. One finally said yes.
In 2012, Forbes called her the youngest self-made female billionaire in the world.

shorts.title: The Sale That Paid for Tesla and SpaceX
shorts.description: In 2002, eBay bought PayPal for $1.5 billion. Elon Musk put almost all of his share into two risky companies.
sources: Wikipedia: Elon Musk — early investments in SpaceX and Tesla

scenes.text: In 2002, eBay bought PayPal for one and a half billion dollars.
One of its biggest shareholders, Elon Musk, got around one hundred and eighty million.
Most people would retire. He didn't.
He put almost all of it into two companies everyone thought would fail: a rocket company and an electric car company.
In 2008, both were close to running out of money.
Both survived. SpaceX and Tesla made him one of the richest people on Earth. Would you have risked it all?

shorts.title: America's 'Most Innovative Company' Was a Fraud
shorts.description: Fortune named Enron America's most innovative company six years in a row. Then it collapsed.

scenes.text: For six years in a row, Fortune called Enron America's most innovative company.
It was one of the biggest energy companies in the United States.
But a lot of its profits weren't real. Debts were hidden in side companies with clever accounting.
In 2001, the truth came out. The stock went from around ninety dollars to under one dollar.
Enron went bankrupt. Thousands lost their jobs and retirement savings.
The most innovative thing about it was the accounting.

shorts.title: Google Used to Be Called BackRub
shorts.description: Before it was Google, Larry Page and Sergey Brin's search engine had a very different name.

scenes.text: Google's first name was… BackRub.
In 1996, Larry Page and Sergey Brin built a search engine at Stanford that ranked pages by their backlinks.
Back links. BackRub. That was the name.
Then they wanted something bigger. They chose googol, the number one followed by one hundred zeros.
As the story goes, it was misspelled, and Google stuck.
Would you search on BackRub?

shorts.title: Twitter Was a Side Project of a Dying Startup
shorts.description: Twitter came out of Odeo, a podcast company crushed when Apple added podcasts to iTunes.
sources: Wikipedia: Twitter — history; acquisition by Elon Musk, 2022

scenes.text: Twitter was born because Apple killed a startup.
In 2005, a company called Odeo was building a podcast platform.
Then Apple put podcasts right inside iTunes. Odeo was finished.
So the team looked for a new idea. One of them proposed short status updates by text message.
In 2006, it became Twitter.
In 2022, Elon Musk bought it for forty four billion dollars. One failure can start something huge.

shorts.title: Slack Came From a Failed Video Game
shorts.description: A game called Glitch flopped. The chat tool its team built for themselves sold for $27.7 billion.
sources: Wikipedia: Slack Technologies — acquired by Salesforce, 2021

scenes.text: Slack exists because a video game failed.
Stewart Butterfield's company was building an online game called Glitch.
Not enough people played it. In 2012, they shut it down.
But while making it, the team had built their own internal chat tool.
They turned that tool into a product and called it Slack.
In 2021, Salesforce bought it for twenty seven point seven billion dollars. Look at what you build along the way.

shorts.title: YouTube Started as a Dating Site 😳
shorts.description: YouTube's first idea was video dating. A year and a half later, Google bought it for $1.65 billion.
sources: Jawed Karim, talk at SXSW 2016, on the dating-site origin

scenes.text: The site you're watching right now started as a dating website.
In early 2005, YouTube's founders had an idea: people upload videos about themselves to find a date.
Nobody uploaded dating videos.
So they opened it up to any video at all.
Around a year and a half later, Google bought YouTube for one point six five billion dollars.
Today, billions of people use it. Sometimes the first idea is just the door.

shorts.title: Coca-Cola Changed Its Recipe… and People Revolted
shorts.description: In 1985, Coca-Cola launched New Coke. 79 days later, the old recipe was back.

scenes.text: In 1985, Coca-Cola changed its secret recipe.
Pepsi was winning taste tests, so Coke made a sweeter formula. In blind tests, people liked it.
But when it hit stores, people were furious. They wanted the original back.
The company got a flood of angry calls and letters. Some fans stockpiled the old Coke.
After just seventy nine days, the original returned as Coca-Cola Classic.
Sales went up. Some still wonder if it was all a genius plan. What do you think?

shorts.title: Wrigley's Gum Started as a Free Gift 🍬
shorts.description: William Wrigley Jr. gave away gum to sell baking powder. Customers wanted the gum.

scenes.text: Wrigley's gum started as a free gift.
In 1891, William Wrigley Junior moved to Chicago to sell soap.
To sell more, he gave away free baking powder with each order.
The baking powder was more popular than the soap. So he sold that, and gave away free chewing gum.
Then people wanted the gum more than the baking powder.
So he sold gum, and Wrigley became one of the biggest gum companies in the world. Watch what customers actually want.

shorts.title: Toyota Started by Making Weaving Looms
shorts.description: Before cars, the Toyoda family built automatic looms. Selling a loom patent helped fund the car business.

scenes.text: Toyota didn't start with cars. It started with weaving machines.
Sakichi Toyoda was an inventor who built automatic looms in Japan.
His best loom stopped by itself when a thread broke. It was a huge deal.
In 1929, the rights to that loom were sold to a British company.
His son Kiichiro used that money to help start building cars.
Today, Toyota is one of the biggest car makers in the world. All thanks to a loom.

shorts.title: The Nike Logo Cost $35 ✔️
shorts.description: In 1971, a student designed the Nike swoosh for $35. Phil Knight wasn't even sure he liked it.

scenes.text: One of the most famous logos on Earth cost thirty five dollars.
In 1971, Phil Knight needed a logo for his new shoe brand.
He asked Carolyn Davidson, a design student, to make one.
She drew the swoosh. Knight said: I don't love it, but it will grow on me.
Years later, Nike gave her a gold ring with the swoosh and shares in the company.
Today that swoosh is worth billions. Would you take thirty five dollars for it?

shorts.title: Pepsi Went Bankrupt Twice
shorts.description: Before it became a giant, Pepsi went bankrupt twice and was nearly sold to its biggest rival.

scenes.text: Pepsi went bankrupt. Twice.
The first time was in 1923, after sugar prices went crazy.
It was sold, and in 1931 it went bankrupt again.
Then Charles Guth, the boss of a candy store chain, bought it. As the story goes, Pepsi was even offered to Coca-Cola. Coke said no.
Pepsi survived by selling bigger bottles for the same price: twice as much for a nickel.
Today, it's one of the biggest food and drink companies in the world.

shorts.title: He Traded Half of Domino's for a Used Car 🚗
shorts.description: Tom Monaghan's brother swapped his half of a small pizzeria for a Volkswagen Beetle.

scenes.text: This man traded half of Domino's for a used car.
In 1960, brothers Tom and James Monaghan bought a small pizzeria in Michigan.
Pretty soon, James wanted out.
So he gave Tom his half of the business… in exchange for a Volkswagen Beetle.
Tom kept going, renamed it Domino's, and built it into a giant.
In 1998, he sold most of it for about one billion dollars. Would you have kept the car?
